title: Fastest Finish With Prerequisites
statement:
A build has n tasks, numbered 0 to n − 1. Task i takes time[i] minutes. Each pair [a, b] in deps means task a must be finished before task b may start. The dependencies never form a cycle.

Any number of tasks can run at the same time, and a task may start the moment all of its dependencies are done. Return the least number of minutes until every task has finished.

(The original numbers tasks from 1; here they are numbered from 0.)

examples.why: Task 2 waits for the slower of 0 and 1, so it starts at 5, ends at 7, and task 3 ends at 11.
Without dependencies everything runs in parallel, so the answer is the longest single task, not the sum.
The chain with the most tasks (0 → 1 → 2) takes 3 minutes; the shorter chain 3 → 4 takes 4. Count minutes, not steps.

constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n, a ≠ b, no repeated pair
hints: When does a task finish at the earliest? Write it in terms of the finish times of its dependencies.
finish[b] = time[b] + max(finish[a]) over all dependencies a of b. You need every dependency's finish time before computing b's. Which ordering of a DAG guarantees that?

Process tasks in topological order (Kahn's algorithm with in-degrees). When you pop a task, push its finish time forward to each dependent as a candidate start time. The answer is the largest finish time.

explain.intuition:
Since tasks can run in parallel without limit, a task starts exactly when its slowest dependency ends: finish[b] = time[b] + max(finish[a]) over its dependencies. The answer is the largest finish time. This is the longest path in a DAG, weighted by node times: the "critical path" from project planning.

The only difficulty is evaluating that formula in an order where every dependency is ready. A topological order does exactly that. With Kahn's algorithm, keep an in-degree per task, start with tasks that have none, and when a task finishes, offer its finish time to each dependent as a possible start. A dependent joins the queue once its last dependency has reported, so its start time is final at that point. It is the same idea as a bundler waiting for every imported module before it can process a file.
steps: Build the adjacency list and in-degree count from deps.
Set start[i] = 0 for every task and queue all tasks with in-degree 0.
Pop task u, set finish = start[u] + time[u], and update the answer.
For each dependent v: start[v] = max(start[v], finish), lower its in-degree, and queue it when it reaches 0.
pitfalls: Summing all the times, as if tasks ran one at a time.
Measuring the longest chain by number of tasks rather than by minutes, as in the third example.
Recursive DFS on a 50 000-task chain can overflow the call stack in JavaScript and Python. The queue-based version has no recursion.

solutions.title: Relax until nothing changes
solutions.idea: Start every finish time at time[i]. Repeatedly push finish[a] + time[b] into finish[b] for every dependency until a full pass changes nothing.

solutions.title: Topological order (Kahn) with earliest start times
solutions.idea: Process tasks once all their dependencies are done; each finished task raises the earliest start of its dependents.

followups: Only k tasks may run at once. Does the problem stay easy? (It becomes NP-hard in general.)
Return the critical path itself, the chain of tasks that decides the total. What do you store per task?
